alternative: Keep strong references only where ownership is real and rely on the engine's GC: model caches and back-references with WeakMap/WeakSet/WeakRef, treat FinalizationRegistry callbacks as non-essential cleanup only, and release external resources deterministically with using/Symbol.dispose or a try/finally.
idiom_name: none - GC owns memory; WeakMap/WeakRef for non-owning edges, using/Symbol.dispose for resources
implementation_notes: JavaScript has no destructors and no ownership types: a wrapper cannot observe or influence when the object it references is reclaimed, and the specification deliberately makes collection timing unobservable, so a hand-built smart pointer only adds indirection over a reference that is already an owning handle. What replaces the classic structure: WeakMap and WeakSet (entries that die with their keys) plus WeakRef (a reference that does not keep its target alive) for edges that must not own; FinalizationRegistry for cleanup that is explicitly not program logic; and using with Symbol.dispose for deterministic teardown of resources at scope exit. Where a strong reference is wanted, an ordinary binding is the handle.
pitfalls: WeakMap/WeakSet keys must be objects and are not enumerable by design, so weak caches cannot be listed, sized or flushed; a plain Map with an eviction policy is sometimes the honest answer.
WeakRef.deref() may return the target even when nothing else holds it, and may return undefined later in the same task; never cache a deref result across awaits or event-loop turns.
FinalizationRegistry callbacks may run late or never (process exit, unreachable registry) and must not carry essential logic; the registry also keeps the held value strongly.
using disposes at scope exit, but the value can escape through closures, returns or globals - re-wrap it at the consumer or use try/finally.
